paras: The Congress saloon fight between Patrolman Flannigan and Joe Baskerville was a brawl in Seattle, Washington, early on Friday, August 11, 1905, in which a police officer threatened to shoot a Black porter and was beaten unconscious by him. Both men were arrested, and the Seattle Star later counted the officer among four patrolmen 'victims' of that week.

Baskerville was a porter at the Congress saloon at Fifth and Pike, and witnesses alleged that Patrolman "Nick" Flannigan, who worked nights, was intoxicated when he came in at about six in the morning.

According to those witnesses, Flannigan demanded a free pint of whisky, cursed bartender Patrick Jennings when he refused, and offered to thrash both the bartender and the porter. When Baskerville offered to fight him alone, Flannigan, in the paper's words, "crawfished and pulled a gun." Baskerville knocked him down once the gun was pocketed, then took both the gun and a brass knuckle the officer struck him with, and drove him to the sidewalk.

Officers Kent and Day arrested both men, who were bleeding heavily, and Chief Delaney said he would investigate. Three days later the Star reported that one of four officers in that week's incidents had been found "clearly at fault" and suspended, without naming him; no report of charges appears in the coverage.

The only coverage found was in the Seattle Star, whose front-page headline, "Officer Is Licked By a Negro Porter," named the porter's race while the story followed witnesses who blamed the drunken officer. On August 14 the paper's front-page box listed Flannigan as a "victim," "assaulted" by Baskerville, "colored porter." No coverage was found in the Black press.
The Star's two treatments assign blame differently: the eyewitness report of August 11 made Flannigan the aggressor, while the one-line August 14 summary made him the victim.

reader.title: Congress saloon fight between Patrolman Flannigan and Joe Baskerville
bases: According to witnesses quoted by the Seattle Star, an intoxicated patrolman threatened to shoot a Black porter, drew a gun and struck him with a brass knuckle before the porter beat him (A1, A2); no mob was involved, and the paper's later box framed the officer as the victim of an assault (A3).
All coverage comes from one paper, the Seattle Star, in a two-part report of Aug. 11 (A1, A2) and a summary box of Aug. 14 (A3); no other paper, white or Black, was found.

accounts.label: Witnesses of the fight (Seattle Star report)
accounts.gist: Flannigan, drunk, demanded free whisky, cursed the bartender, offered to thrash him and the porter, then 'crawfished' and pulled a gun when Baskerville offered to fight him alone; Baskerville knocked him down only after he pocketed the gun.

accounts.label: Seattle Star summary box
accounts.gist: Lists Flannigan as the third of four patrolmen 'victims', 'assaulted' by Baskerville, and says one of the four officers was at fault and suspended.

framing.detail: The Star's headline 'Officer Is Licked By a Negro Porter' foregrounded the porter's race, while the story relayed witnesses who blamed the drunken officer and called him 'game'; the Aug. 14 box cast Flannigan as a 'victim' of assault in a week of attacks on police.

versions.value: Baskerville was threatened with a gun and struck with a brass knuckle by the officer, who started the trouble (witnesses)

conflicts.note: Both versions come from the same paper; the Aug. 11 report rests on named-location eyewitness detail, while the Aug. 14 box is a one-line summary that also says one unnamed officer was at fault and suspended.
